We examined 60 columns across 5 data files.
#### Issues Identified

3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 5 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Mouthings -mouth movements that mimic spoken language words produced alongside signing -are a unique multimodal phenomenon in that they recruit resources from a second language; however, they have not received much attention in research that explicitly frames itself as multimodal.
In Norwegian Sign Language (NSL/NTS), the role of mouthing in comprehension has not been studied extensively from the perspective of deaf users of the language.
In this study, we add to these two understudied areas by exploring mouthings in comprehension of Norwegian Sign Language in an unrestricted lexical identification paradigm (N=30).
We find that when manual forms are polysemous, plausible mouthings improve accuracy in lexical identification and the certainty of comprehension.
When mouthings are implausible, it appears that the dominant strategy is to make identification decisions based on the manual form only.
In a smaller number of cases participants appeared to rely solely on the mouthing or blended the mouthing and manual components.
What is the effect of the presence of multiple information streams in comprehension in language and certainty in that comprehension?
We consider this question by examining how Norwegianlinked mouthing in Norwegian Sign Language (NSL)1 contributes to identification of decontextualized signs in the manual channel.
Mouthings are mouth patterns that mimic spoken language words, produced with or without vocalisation, that are layered over manual signing (Bisnath 2024).

text.text: We begin with a brief overview of mouthing in general (Section 2) and mouthing in NSL (Section 3).
We present the method (Section 4) and findings (Section 5), and contextualise our findings in the literature on NSL, comprehension and multimodality (Section 5).
Throughout the paper manual elements are marked with small capitals and mouthing elements in bolded italics, as in MANUAL+mouthing.

The following terms also in small capitals are not signs, but labels: CONGRUENT, MORPHO-PHONOLOGICAL, INITIALISED, MORPHO-SYNTACTIC, POLYSEMOUS, INI-TIALISED, HOMOPHONE, CORRECT-PHON, WRONG-LOC, ZERO, MATCHED, MISMATCHED.
All manual forms used as stimuli are polysemous, but are identified with a single Norwegian gloss for the sake of simplicity.
These glosses should be understood as referring to a specific phonological form and not meaning.
Exceptions are cases in the MATCHED condition in which a mouthing narrows down the polysemy in the manual form.
We use the term mouthing to refer to mouth patterns that are recognisable as mimicking spoken language words, produced with or without vocalisation, during signing.
This definition centers language contact and does not mean that signers necessarily consider mouthing to be exclusively part of a spoken language.

text.text: Four of the most common forms of mouthing construction are CONGRUENT, MORPHO-PHONOLOGICAL (with subtypes POLYSEMOUS, INITIALISED and HOMOPHONE), MORPHO-SYNTACTIC and FREE (Bisnath 2024).

text.text: We describe these forms briefly here to provide a framework for discussing mouthing and refer readers to Bisnath (2024) for examples.

text.text: CONGRUENT mouthings can be glossed in the same way as the manual form they accompany.
MORPHO-PHONOLOGICAL identifies a group of constructions that share the same manual form that is specified by mouthings.

MORPHO-P r e p r i n t Correspondence: fbisnath@umich.edu PHONOLOGICAL sub-types differ in how group members relate to each other -constructions in the POLYSEMOUS group have similar meaning, INITIALISED use the same manual alphabet handshape as the written form of their mouthing begins with the same letter, and HOMOPHONES are related by chance.
In MORPHO-SYNTACTIC constructions, the mouthing contributes propositional content and so, for example, can act as complement of the manual form it is associated with.
Lastly, FREE mouthings are those that are not clearly associated with a manual sign temporally i.e. they may be produced in the transition between signs.
Across the four constructions, the stability of the form of the mouthing component is assumed to be graded as follows: MORPHO-PHONOLOGICAL > CONGRUENT, MORPHO-SYNTACTIC > FREE.
text.formatted: Across the four constructions, the stability of the form of the mouthing component is assumed to be graded as follows: MORPHO-PHONOLOGICAL > CONGRUENT, MORPHO-SYNTACTIC > FREE.

text.text: MORPHO-PHONOLOGICAL mouthings are likely most conventionalised because they disambiguate identical manual forms.
FREE mouthings are least conventionalised as they can take on any form.
CONGRUENT and MORPHO-SYNTACTIC constructions fall in between as are they are constrained in some ways by properties of their manual component.
Furthermore, CONGRUENT mouthings are likely not always produced while MORPHO-SYNTACTIC constructions could have manual-only alternates.
Experimental studies can isolate mouthing and thus demonstrate how it specifically is implicated in sign language comprehension.

Deaf signers of French Sign Language (LSF) use the manual and mouthing components of CONGRUENT mouthing constructions together in lexical retrieval, and are slower to identify a sign and more inaccurate when mouthing is unexpected (either a pseudo-word or semantically-incongruent) (Bogliotti & Isel 2021).

text.text: Together these findings show that users of sign languages in western industrialised countries do use mouthing to identify decontextualised signs and particularly rely on it when manual forms are ambiguous.
The Italian Sign Language signers' viewing patterns suggest that noisy mouthing conditions (blurring) create uncertainty.

Norwegian Sign Language (NSL) is the national sign language of Norway used by approximately 16,500 people, 3000-3500 of whom are deaf (Norwegian Deaf Association).
The majority spoken language is Norwegian, in which dialectal variation is institutionally accepted and can be written with two systems (Bokmål and Nynorsk).
Major deaf centers are found in Oslo and Ål in the east, Bergen in the west, and Trondheim in the middle (and north of the other cities).
Two dialects linked to Oslo and Trondheim are named in the literature (Greftegreff et al. 2015), and 255 signs specific to Northern Sámi-using regions have been recorded (Haualand et al. 2023).

text.text: In NSL, mouthing (munnstillinger, munnbevegelser, ordbilder in Norwegian) was described relatively early in the study of sign languages, but has not received much explicit treatment more recently.
Mouthing is described as so strongly integrated into NSL that it is perceived as obligatory in marking certain meaning differences (Haualand et al. 2023).

In terms of distribution, mouthings are most likely to be found at the beginning of narratives and dialogues.

They are primarily nouns and bare verbs and much less commonly derived verbs or classifier predicates (Vogt-Svendsen 2001). Anible & Bisnath (n.d.) shows a related pattern, finding that mouthing is more likely to occur with lexical signs as opposed to depicting ones (classifier constructions).

text.text: In more recent work, Arnold (2024) identifies additional cases of CONGRUENT mouthing, particularly of wh-words, potential cases of MORPHO-PHONOLOGICAL and MORPHO-SYNTACTIC mouthing, and FREE mouthing.
The potential MORPHO-PHONOLOGICAL case is of WHERE being used with hva ('what') and hvor ('where') mouthing to signal the respective interrogatives.
There is also a case in which TEGN3 ('sign') and the mouthing bruke ('use') co-occur in a larger utterance asking an interlocutor to specify the sign they used for a concept.
The mouthing on its own can be interpreted as specifying the predicate of the utterance, thus acting as part of a MORPHO-SYNTACTIC mouthing construction.
A phrasal FREE mouthing example is Hva sa du?

text.text: The study is oriented around the following research question: Are NSL signers more accurate and certain at identifying POLYSEMOUS manual forms when they are produced with a plausible mouthing compared to without?
The overarching motivation is to examine how language users make use of semiotic resources, regardless of modality and named language association, in comprehension.
We focus on POLYSEMOUS constructions as their manual element is ambiguous without mouthing leading us to expect that their mouthing is most conventionalised (recall Section 2).

This makes them a good candidate for showing the role of mouthing in lexical identification as we can assume that signers might expect to see this kind mouthing and respond differently when they do not.
Subsequent sections describe the task and stimulus design and predictions.

The test items are manual forms that are ambiguous without mouthing, or fall into Bisnath (2024)'s MORPHO-PHONOLOGICAL mouthing type.

An example of this is the 5-claw handshape produced on the cheek with short repeated twists, which, when produced with the mouthing tomat ('tomato'), is a sign for tomato, and when produced with the mouthing eple ('apple') is a sign for apple.

The test items are produced in three mouthing conditions: (i) MATCHED, plausible mouthing for manual form e.g. tomat (ii) ZERO, no mouthing (iii) MISMATCHED, real Norwegian words that are unlikely to appear with the manual form in citation form (see examples in Table 1).
text.formatted: The test items are produced in three mouthing conditions: (i) MATCHED, plausible mouthing for manual form e.g. tomat (ii) ZERO, no mouthing (iii) MISMATCHED, real Norwegian words that are unlikely to appear with the manual form in citation form (see examples in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: A plausible mouthing here refers to one that exists in the Tegnordbok dictionary.

As the manual forms are intentionally chosen to be ambiguous, multiple mouthings could have been paired with the same manual form to create MATCHED items; however for the sake of simplicity, only one mouthing was chosen.
This mouthing was chosen by referencing entries in the Tegnordbok dictionary and the intuitions of the second author.
The manual-mouthing pairs in the dictionary are assumed to be reasonably familiar to NSL signers.
We did this because there is no available database of frequencies of manual-mouthing pairings for NSL (or likely any sign language).

Within the groups that had the same manual form and different mouthings, we chose the mouthing that (i) formed a manual-mouthing pair for concepts that did not have an alternative sign in Tegnordbok according to the second author and (ii) had the highest imageability.
Thus in the grouping EPLE-TOMAT-AUGUST ('apple-tomato-august'), TOMAT is selected because there is another sign for EPLE and it has a higher imageability rating than AUGUST.

The mouthings in the MISMATCHED condition were selected to be either Norwegian verbs or adjectives i.e. not nouns, to begin with a sound that has a different articulation location than the real mouthing, and to have the same number of syllables as the real mouthing.
Thus, the MISMATCHED counterpart of TOMAT has the mouthing høyre ('right').
Correspondence: fbisnath@umich.edu
The fillers are signs judged by the second author to be possible to identify without mouthing.
They are produced in the two location conditions with the same mouthing: (i) CORRECT-PHON, phonologically correct manual form and (ii) WRONG-LOC, produced in wrong location.
Thus tog ('train') in the CORRECT-PHON condition is produced with the bent-n handshape, oriented with the palm up, in neutral space with tog mouthing.
In the WRONG-LOC condition it is produced in the same way except above the head.
The WRONG-LOC condition was created as a phonological foil to the ZERO condition.
Given the prevalence of mouthing in NSL, we assumed that manual forms are produced with mouthing by default, making the ZERO condition phonologically questionable at minimum.
The sample consists of 35 deaf and hard-of-hearing participants who said they had done the experiment once, and defined themselves as knowing NSL very well or fluently.

Participants are heterogeneous in their age (m=38, M =35, sd=13.5, min=19, max=77), age-of-onset of NSL (m=2.6, M =1, sd=4.2, min=0, max=16), and years spent participating in the deaf community (m=34.6, M =35.5, sd=16.1, min=0, max=65).
The resulting ratings and open responses were analysed quantitatively and qualitatively respectively.
To assess accuracy, the second author examined all the open-response answers given alongside the relevant stimuli and determined if the answer was plausible.
She examined the responses given and determined if her interpretation of the manual-mouthing constructions she produced could be interpreted to be the concept given as a response.
We took this route as the stimuli had relatively natural mouthing i.e. not highly-emphasised, and thus the same mouthform could be associated with multiple words.

The average number of allowable answers by condition is as follows: MATCHED (1.4) < MIS-MATCHED (2.6) < ZERO (3.3); thus the threshold for accuracy is highest in the MATCHED condition (see examples of MATCHED = 1-3, ZERO = 4-6 and MISMATCHED = 7-9 in Table 1 below).

text.text: The average number of plausible answers for MATCHED is not 1, as one might expect, due to cases 1 to 3.
In 1 and 2, the answers given are semantically-related and so were considered acceptable.
We asked participants to only give nouns as answers, but ultimately included other grammatical categories (klype, 'pinch'; elektrisk, 'electric') due to their semantic relatedness.
Metall ('metal') was accepted as an option for MIDDAG+middag because it has the same number of syllables and begins with the same form (/m/) (future studies should exclude this item).

In the case of 7, SØPPEL ('garbage'), without mouthing, its form can be interpreted as profiling the hands performing an action as in kaste ('to throw') or droppe ('to drop'), or as reflecting visual perception as in lys ('light').
Examples 7 to 9 are answers that were accepted as accurate even though conceptually the stimuli should not have any right answer.

We examined the answers given to MISMATCHED stimuli, regardless of if they were judged as accurate, as they can give insight into how participants bring together mouthing and manual components to name a construction.
After removing cases in which participants did not give a response, 96 remained.
The distribution of these categories per stimulus is shown in Figure 4 and examples in Figure 5.

text.text: The first clear pattern is that the type of response given varies across stimulus items.
So, for example BJØRN+gul primarily elicited responses that drew on the manual only, while BUNAD+glemme could be interpreted as drawing on the manual and mouthing components.
BATTERI+morsom also elicited only responses that drew on the manual component, 7The model initially included a random effect of participant; however there was no variance at this level.

text.text: The overwhelmingly dominant strategy was to give an answer that could align with the manual component as in banan ('banana') for PØLSE+grave and kontakt ('contact') for BATTERI+morsom -this occurred for all stimulus items and was generally the most frequent strategy per item.
The second most common strategy was to give a response that resembled the mouthing element only as in ferdig for KOFFERT+ferdig and merke for SUPPE+melke.
The third most common was to seemingly blend of the mouthing and manual components as in the responses legeme ('human body') and kappe ('robe') for BUNAD+glemme.

The least used strategy was to give a response that did not seem to be phonologically related to the the manual and mouthing components individually or together as in excel for SØPPEL+henge and vedtak ('decision') for KOFFERT+ferdig.

In this study we aimed to expand understanding of how a cue that has received little attention in multimodality studies -mouthing -contributes to comprehension.
We did this by examining an extreme case in NSL, that of POLYSEMOUS mouthing constructions -groups of signs with the same manual form disambiguated by mouthings.

We innovated on existing lexical identification paradigms by allowing for open responses, thus making it possible to gain insight into how participants might be bringing together mouthing and manual elements.
Our quasi-experimental approach was useful in that it likely increased participant recruitment, but did not allow for more precise and/or indirect behavioural measures, like reaction time.
Instead we opted for explicitly asking participants for certainty ratings, which were able to distinguish between the conditions.

For researchers interested in recruiting larger and more diverse participant samples in contexts similar to that of Norway (geographically dispersed, industrialised), designs such as ours may be necessary.
In the following we situate our findings in the literature on sign languages and co-speech gesture and our methodological contributions.

The significant difference in accuracy between the MATCHED and MISMATCHED constructions demonstrates that NSL signers are actively attending to mouthing when identifying signs, at least when presented in a decontextualised task viewed on a screen.

Lowered accuracy and certainty with MISMATCHED constructions suggests that comprehenders have phonological and/or P r e p r i n t Correspondence: fbisnath@umich.edu semantic expectations linked to the mouthing component that can be disturbed, as evidenced by responses that roughly translate to '...but mouth was different' and 'funny in mouthing...' to MIS-MATCHED items.
This would be expected for MORPHO-PHONOLOGICAL mouthing constructions as definitionally there should be a limited number of allowable mouthings.

That the Norwegian participants minimally attend to mouthing aligns with existing research on NSL and with studies of other sign languages showing that deaf signers tend to look at the face, as opposed to the hands, when viewing videos of signing (Agrafiotis et al. 2003). Gappmayr (2026)'s experimental studies of fingerspelling with and without mouthing in American Sign Language adds some specificity, showing deaf perceivers look to the face more often when mouthing is present.

text.text: A caveat to this is that deaf signers' looking behaviour may be different in face-to-face interaction as early-exposed American Sign Language signers tend to look between the eyes while adult sign language learners tend to look at the mouth (Emmorey et al. 2009).
text.formatted: A caveat to this is that deaf signers' looking behaviour may be different in face-to-face interaction as early-exposed American Sign Language signers tend to look between the eyes while adult sign language learners tend to look at the mouth <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Emmorey et al. 2009</ref>).

text.text: It is also not clear what differences there may be when viewing videos on computer screens vs. mobile phones -in the present experiment it was possible to do both.

These findings suggest that the mouthing element is broadly analogous to co-speech gestures that resolve ambiguous spoken statements (Hinnell & Parrill 2020), allowing for differences in ambiguity across sentences vs. words/signs and mouthings vs. gestures.
text.formatted: These findings suggest that the mouthing element is broadly analogous to co-speech gestures that resolve ambiguous spoken statements <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Hinnell & Parrill 2020)</ref>, allowing for differences in ambiguity across sentences vs. words/signs and mouthings vs. gestures.

text.text: Mouthings may represent an intersection between iconic and emblematic gestures as their form reflects that of spoken words which belong to larger symbolic systems.

However, much is left to be theorised about the comparability of mouthing in sign languages and co-speech gesture; doing so would be a useful means of including the practices of deaf populations in understandings of multimodality in language.
Qualitative analysis of MISMATCHED stimuli suggests that signers might prefer to ignore the mouthing element when presented with isolated polysemous manual forms and unlikely mouthings.
In fact, they largely behave as they do with ZERO stimulus items.
This seems to be the case when banan is a response for PØLSE+grave as variants of BANAN and PØLSE are POLYSEMOUS mouthing constructions (with potential minor phonetic differences in Figure 5a).
text.formatted: This seems to be the case when banan is a response for PØLSE+grave as variants of BANAN and PØLSE are POLYSEMOUS mouthing constructions (with potential minor phonetic differences in Figure <ref type="figure">5a</ref>).

text.text: However, it is important to note that the same mouthing could correspond to multiple Norwegian words and can be further complicated by dialectal variation in Norwegian.
This variation likely cannot fully explain why a mouthing of grave could be interpreted as banan, but this is an empirical question to be considered in the future.
What could it mean that signers appear to be drawing on mouthing in sign identification in some cases?
In Figure 5c, we see an instance in which klemme ('hug') is given as a response for BUNAD+glemme despite the differences in the manual components of BUNAD and KLEMME.
text.formatted: In Figure <ref type="figure">5c</ref>, we see an instance in which klemme ('hug') is given as a response for BUNAD+glemme despite the differences in the manual components of BUNAD and KLEMME.

text.text: A potential reason is that manual forms with the same location may be perceived as similar; this is reported in American Sign Language (Hildebrandt & Corina 2002), but has not yet been explored in NSL.

text.text: Such an explanation however cannot account for cases like Figure 5b in which the manual form of the test item and the participant's response differ in all parameters.

text.text: Clearly the findings of this study do not reflect comprehension in in-person communication.

That is, we do not expect that polysemous signs remain so as a conversation proceeds and we expect that participants will signal that they need clarification if they are not understanding something (Skedsmo 2020a).
text.formatted: That is, we do not expect that polysemous signs remain so as a conversation proceeds and we expect that participants will signal that they need clarification if they are not understanding something <ref type="bibr">(Skedsmo 2020a</ref>).

text.text: However, this study quantifies the pieces that context may need to fill when elements like mouthing are absent or obscured.
Future work should consider the role of mouthing in comprehension of manual forms that are not typically polysemous (CONGRUENT mouthing) as well as mouthing in sentential and conversational contexts.
This study describes the use of a multimodal multilingual phenomenon -mouthing -in comprehension of a sign language.
It demonstrates that Norwegian mouthings aid lexical identification and certainty of comprehension for deaf users of Norwegian Sign Language.
Similar findings have been made in other sign languages regarding mouthing specifically, and more broadly with co-speech gesture.
This study makes a novel contribution in identifying potential ways in which comprehenders might bring together manual and mouthing components.
The most common strategy appears to be to ignore the mouthing element when it might be viewed as conflicting with the manual form, suggesting prioritisation of the manual channel in comprehension.
